extracted.intended_audience: scientists, statisticians, schoolmasters, and general readers interested in anthropometry/psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Methods for ordering, comparing, and recording individuals and groups (centesimal grading, quantile comparison) and observational procedures for studying character, criminality, insanity, and social instincts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of two large statistical groups
rubrics_metrics.description: When we desire to compare any two large statistical groups, we may compare median with median, quartiles with quartiles, and octiles with octiles; or we may proceed on the method to be described in the next paragraph but one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either compare corresponding quantiles directly, or use the alternative centesimal-grade correspondence method (stating the centesimal grade in one group that corresponds with the median or any other fractional grade in the other). This latter method is simple, theory-independent, and applicable wherever sorting in order is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and treatment of centesimal grade (rank vs graduation)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is most conformable to usage to give an individual's centesimal grade—his place on the base line AB graduated from 0° to 100°. In reckoning this, a confusion ought to be avoided between 'graduation' and 'rank' ... all intermediate ranks stand half a degree short of the graduation bearing the same number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When converting discrete ranks into a 0–100 scale, treat each rank as located at (rank − 0.5) in the original division before rescaling; when classes are large the half-place difference is negligible and rank and graduation may be treated as identical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical calculation of centesimal position (examples/Rule of Three)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: A child No.5 in class of 27 ⇒ rank corresponds to graduation 4°.5; rescale to 100: x : 4°.5 :: 100 : 27; x = 450°/27 = 16°.6. Another child No.13 in class of 25 ⇒ rank 12°.5; x : 12°.5 :: 100 : 25; x = 1250°/25 = 50° (the median).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert rank to graduation by subtracting 0.5, then use proportional scaling (Rule of Three) to map to a centesimal (0–100) scale; this yields a centesimal grade usable for cross-group comparisons (e.g., expressing that 16°.6 in one class equals 50° in another).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pocket pricker method for rapid comparative records
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a fine pricker (modified small pencil-case with a short needle) and a scrap of paper perforated by the needle; arrange the paper to present three distinct compartments to the pricker corresponding to 'more', 'equal to', or 'less'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tear the paper into the form of a cross (maimed in one arm) so the head receives 'more' pricks, the solitary unmaimed arm 'the same', and the long foot 'less'. Write the subject of measurement on the paper beforehand so multiple records can be kept separately and added to later; perforations are easily counted by holding paper to the light. This enables unobtrusive, tactile recording in public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of schoolchildren and teacher observation for studying character proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: The varieties of character ... have never yet been investigated. The necessary observations ought, however, to be easily made on young children in schools, whose manifestations of character are conspicuous, who are simultaneously for months and years under the eye of the same master or mistress, and who are daily classed according to their various merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach the subject wholly without prejudice (as pure observation), use long-term observations by the same teacher to record proportions of character types, and consult experienced teachers for obvious divisions of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key observable character dimensions to record
rubrics_metrics.description: Replies from experienced teachers emphasised divisions of character connected with energy, sociability, desire to attract notice, truthfulness, thoroughness, and refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying or recording 'character' in children, prioritize observable traits such as energy, sociability, attention-seeking, honesty, diligence, and refinement as initial categories for statistical investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral indicators associated with criminality
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal criminal has marked peculiarities of character: his conscience is almost deficient, his instincts are vicious, his power of self-control is very weak, and he usually detests continuous labour. The deficiency of conscience in criminals, as shown by the absence of genuine remorse for their guilt, ... hypocrisy is a very common vice; and all my information agrees as to the utter untruthfulness of criminals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing criminal tendencies observationally or in institutional records, look for lack of remorse, habitual untruthfulness, weak self-control, aversion to steady labour, and vicious instincts; consider temper, passion, or intellectual imbecility as proximate causes of poor self-control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedigree and heredity investigation of criminal classes
rubrics_metrics.description: The perpetuation of the criminal class by heredity is a question difficult to grapple with on many accounts. Their vagrant habits, their illegitimate unions, and extreme untruthfulness, are among the difficulties of the investigation. Example: the Jukes family pedigree tracing many generations and tabulating convictions, pauperism, intemperance, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace large pedigrees across generations to assess hereditary tendencies, but account for ascertainment biases and social confounders (vagrancy, illegitimacy, reporting/untruthfulness). Use careful aggregation (e.g., multi-generation counts of jailings, pauperism, disease) and note limits of inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observable signs and phases of epilepsy and insanity
rubrics_metrics.description: The criminal classes contain a considerable portion of epileptics and other persons of instable, emotional temperament, subject to nervous explosions ... In the confirmed epileptic constitution the signs of general instability of nervous action are muscular convulsions, irregularities of bodily temperature, mobile intellectual activity, and extraordinary oscillations between opposed emotional states. Madness ... includes phases such as strange views about individuality and gloomy segregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record physiological and behavioral markers (convulsions, temperature irregularities, rapid swings of affect, contradictory piety/vice) and social behavior (isolation, moody segregation) as part of character/psychopathology observation; recognize associations between fasting/celibacy and induced morbid states historically reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary reasoning about gregarious and slavish instincts
rubrics_metrics.description: The vast majority of persons of our race have a natural tendency to shrink from the responsibility of standing and acting alone; the slavish aptitudes ... are a direct consequence of his gregarious nature ... gregarious brutes possess a want of self-reliance ... natural selection tends to give but one leader to each suitably-sized herd, and to repress superabundant leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing social or 'slavish' behaviors, consider ecological pressures (predation, herd size, resource distribution) and natural selection consequences (optimal number of leaders per herd). Use comparative observation of animals (e.g., Damara oxen) to infer mechanisms and expected frequency distributions (e.g., ~1 leader per herd-size optimum).
